name: Murphy's Law
description: 'Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong' is a memorable engineering aphorism about planning for failure and edge cases, not a tested behavioral-science finding. In design practice it functions as a resilience mindset more than a psychological law.
design_relevance_note: Often invoked in QA, reliability work, form validation, recovery flows, and failure-mode design: assume edge cases and breakages will happen, so build guardrails and fallbacks accordingly.
myth_risk_note: No empirical validation of a named psychological effect exists; the phrase appears in the literature only as figurative language (e.g., market-anomaly disappearance), not as a tested experimental phenomenon -- popular folklore, comparable to this taxonomy's existing Jakob's/Tesler's/Postel's Law and Law of Triviality entries.
prevalence_note: Culturally ubiquitous across engineering, software, and product-team conversations, and often invoked in resilient-design thinking, even though it is not a formal first-tier UX law.

applications.title: A textbook new-equipment rollout where 'everything that could go wrong, did'
applications.description: A 1991 MIT Sloan Management Review study by Chew, Leonard-Barton, and Bohn documents real manufacturing technology rollouts derailed by unforeseen, compounding failures. In one case, a large aluminum processing plant installed a new 'JRC' electromechanical pump to stir molten metal in a remelt furnace -- a pump already used successfully in over a dozen steel operations and at least one other aluminum foundry. Despite that track record, the silicon nosepiece material turned brittle in the plant's extremely high-temperature baths, the vendor (undergoing internal restructuring) became inattentive, spare parts arrived slowly, and operators -- previously rewarded for loading large batches infrequently -- had to unlearn that habit because the new pump choked on large loads. A second case, a furniture manufacturer's computer-controlled fabric-cutting equipment rollout, separately failed via a different compounding chain: late software, understaffed scheduling changes, oversized cutting tables, forced re-specialization of labor, and nonstandard fabric widths from suppliers degrading downstream sewing quality.
applications.industry_context: heavy manufacturing (aluminum processing) and furniture manufacturing, new production-technology adoption
applications.ethical_note: A researcher-documented account of real operational failure used to derive lessons for technology-adoption planning -- no end-user manipulation involved.
